Aggrega reads one file at your project r: Aggrega reads one file at your project root — `.aggrega-config.yaml`, carrying a `workspace:` block — and climbs to find it, starting at the folder you opened.
Every Aggrega operation runs against a *: Every Aggrega operation runs against a **workspace root** — one folder that the compiler treats as the top of your project. It is where catalog directories are resolved from, where rendered artifacts are written, and what every path in a request is interpreted relative to.
Aggrega's own configuration is **two fil: Aggrega's own configuration is **two files, and most projects need nothing else**:
**One file in your project**, named `.ag: **One file in your project**, named `.aggrega-config.yaml`, sitting at the project root. Its `workspace:` block is what marks the directory as the project root, and a project that vendors no catalog content still writes the block empty — `workspace: {}` — because the block's presence is the marker.
**One global file on your machine**, at: **One global file on your machine**, at `~/.config/aggrega/config.yaml`. It holds settings that belong to the machine rather than to any one project — the registries you pull from and the signature trust policy for each, how large the compiled-module store may grow, and any command-extension plugin you have installed. It loads automatically when it is there, and nothing breaks when it is not.
Between the two files, your project's fi: Between the two files, your project's file wins. Marking the root with a `workspace:` block is the explicit choice and the one to prefer; a project that has never declared one can still be recognised by other markers, so a folder can be a workspace root without carrying that file at all.
Because discovery climbs rather than des: Because discovery climbs rather than descends, the root may legitimately sit *above* the folder you opened. The **{0} ({1})** row at the top of the Commands panel always names the folder that was actually anchored, so when it differs from what you opened you can see why.
That is the whole model for one project: That is the whole model for one project on one machine. Everything else exists for projects that outgrow it — more than one configuration file inside one project, a list that extends what an outer file declared rather than replacing it, a configuration file your pipeline owns, the other ways a project root is recognised, and what a relative path written in a configuration file points at. Aggrega's own configuration reference carries every one of them, and `aggrega config show --origin` names where each setting in force right now came from: a configuration file, an environment variable, or the built-in default.
**{0}** writes the smallest file that an: **{0}** writes the smallest file that anchors a root, in the folder you have open. **{1}** offers the folders beneath you that Aggrega already recognises, and adds the one you choose so the compiler anchors there.

The editor starts the `aggrega` binary n: The editor starts the `aggrega` binary named in your settings; a plain name is looked up on your PATH.
This extension computes nothing about yo: This extension computes nothing about your architecture itself. It renders the compiler's own answers — so a compiler it can start is what everything else here depends on.
Two transports carry those answers, and: Two transports carry those answers, and both run the same binary:
a **language server**, started once and: a **language server**, started once and kept running, which answers validation, navigation, hover, completion, the topology graph and the workspace catalog;
**one-shot commands**, run per operation: **one-shot commands**, run per operation and streamed to the Aggrega output channel, which carry fetching dependencies, the plugin list, generating catalog entities from a plugin, and the Catalog panel's check of one entity.
Which binary runs is the `aggrega.server: Which binary runs is the `aggrega.server.binaryPath` setting. A plain name is looked up on your `PATH`; an absolute or relative path is honoured as written.
That setting is yours rather than the pr: That setting is yours rather than the project's: it names something about the machine you are working on, so a repository cannot pin it for whoever clones it. The consequence is deliberate — a project cannot point this extension at a checked-in build — and it is what lets you keep one path locally and a different one inside a container.
The language server's state is reported: The language server's state is reported in the status bar, on the left. It reads **{0}**, **{1}**, or **{2}**, and its tooltip says which of two reasons applies: nothing here is a folder Aggrega recognises, or there is one and no server is attached to it. Clicking it offers to start or restart.
**{0}** restores the plain name — the pa: **{0}** restores the plain name — the path for someone who installed the compiler after opening the editor. **{1}** selects a build you keep elsewhere.
**{0}** fetches the newest published rel: **{0}** fetches the newest published release this extension works with, built for the machine the editor runs its extensions on — the remote machine, in a window opened on one. It proposes the folder Aggrega's install scripts use, `~/.local/bin` on Linux and macOS and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\aggrega` on Windows, which you can change; it shows the version and asks you to confirm before anything is downloaded, checks the file against the release's published checksums, and then sets `aggrega.server.binaryPath` to it. It never replaces a compiler you put somewhere yourself, and it never upgrades on its own.
Building, previewing and the topology gr: Building, previewing and the topology graph each act on one Release, so the editor needs to know which one you mean.
A **Release** is the document that says: A **Release** is the document that says *this* Aggregate is deployed *here*, with these parameters fulfilled. It is what turns developer intent into something a compiler can render.
So most of what this extension does acts: So most of what this extension does acts on one Release rather than on the workspace in general: validation, building, previewing a build, the topology graph and pulling dependencies all need to know which one you mean. The editor asks once and remembers, rather than asking at every command.
The selection is named in two places — a: The selection is named in two places — a status-bar indicator, and a **{0}** row at the top of the Commands panel — so the Problems panel and the graph always describe the same Release, and you can see which without pressing anything.
Two properties of the selection are wort: Two properties of the selection are worth knowing:
**It is remembered per editor window, no: **It is remembered per editor window, not in the repository.** Your choice does not travel to whoever else opens the project.
**It is re-verified when it is restored.** A Release that no longer resolves falls back to the workspace's own default, and says so — rather than failing on first use, at a moment you cannot connect to a choice made in a previous session.
The Releases offered are the ones the la: The Releases offered are the ones the language server will accept, named relative to the folder it anchored to. Recording a workspace's own persisted default is a separate, explicit act.
**{0}** opens the same drafting flow as: **{0}** opens the same drafting flow as **{1}** at the head of the Catalog panel, with the kind already settled — you are asked for the name and nothing else. **{2}** opens the picker over what this workspace offers.
Pulling dependencies and searching the p: Pulling dependencies and searching the published catalog resolve against the registries your configuration names.
A **registry** is where published catalo: A **registry** is where published catalog content lives — the Components, Features, Recipes and Plugins your Aggregate refers to but does not itself contain.
Two things have nothing to resolve again: Two things have nothing to resolve against without one:
**Pulling dependencies**, which fetches: **Pulling dependencies**, which fetches what a Release refers to and pins it,
**Searching the published catalog**, whi: **Searching the published catalog**, which is how you find an entity to refer to in the first place.
Registries are named by your configurati: Registries are named by your configuration rather than by this extension, and each one carries its own signature trust policy — whether artifacts pulled from it must be signed. The **Registries** panel lists every registry the effective configuration declares, with each one's host, its alias, which is the default, whether signatures are required, and whether a credential for that host is present. Reading that list contacts no registry: the credential state reports presence only, so it says a credential exists rather than that the registry would accept it.
A registry belongs in the global file on: A registry belongs in the global file on your machine rather than in your project's: the registries you pull from are the same wherever you are working, so declaring them once is the point. **Secrets are not configuration** — a registry password and a signing identity token are never fields in either file, and are supplied by environment variable or flag at the moment they are needed.
**{0}** registers the public hub togethe: **{0}** registers the public hub together with its signature trust policy, using the compiler's own seeding — so what you get here and what you would get from the command line are the same configuration. It writes the global file on your machine rather than one in your project. Seeding is for a machine that has no configuration file yet: where one is already there it declines, names the file it found, and leaves that file exactly as it stands.
**{0}** does the same for a host you sup: **{0}** does the same for a host you supply, which is the path for a private or air-gapped hub.
**{0}** is the one to press when a confi: **{0}** is the one to press when a configuration file already exists — including when seeding has just declined and named it. Registering a registry carries no such condition, because the entry is merged into the configuration that is there: every registry you have already declared keeps its entry, and nothing in the file is rewritten. It asks you for the host and for which configuration file to write it to.
